subtopic: WORK OF CANADIAN DELEGATION-DISCUSSIONS ON INTERNATIONAL CONTROL

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): I should like to table two copies of the first report of the atomic energy commission to the security council. While copies for distribution to all members of the house are not at present available, it is hoped to be able to obtain sufficient printed copies shortly.
The last occasion upon which a full statement was made to the house in regard to atomic energy' was on December 17, 1945. when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) described the events leading up to the Washington declaration of November. 1945. In view of the importance of the subject and the length of time which has elapsed. I thought it might be appropriate to make a statement to the house at this time. As this report is only of an interim nature and the discussions on the international control of atomic energy are still in progress, I should like, if it is agreeable to the house, to confine myself to a statement on the work of the Canadian delegation to the atomic energy commission to date, and to indicate the state of the discussions on the international control of atomic energy'. I feel that I need hardly' impress on the house the importance of the subject matter dealt with in this report and as I assume that the members interested in these matters will wish to read this document, I shall only pass in review the various phases in the deliberations of the atomic energy commission leading up to the completion of the report and its transmission to the security council. I shall also outline briefly the situation with regard to the discussions which have taken place on atomic energy in the security council.
As hon. members are aware, the declaration on atomic energy' made in Washington on November 15, 1945 by the President of the United States, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the Prime Minister of Canada urged that at the earliest practicable date a commission of the united nations should be established to prepare recommen-
[Mr. A.bbott.1

Atomic Energy Commission
dations for submission to the united nations. Following a meeting of the foreign ministers of the U.S.S.R., the United States and the United Kingdom in Moscow in December,
1945,	the atomic energy commission of the united nations was established by a resolution of the general assembly of the 24th January,
1946.
The first meeting of the commission took place in New York City on the 14th of June, 1946. The countries represented on the commission from June 14 to December 31, 1946, were Australia, Brazil. China, Canada, Egypt. France, Mexico, the Netherlands, Poland, U.S.S.R., United Kingdom and the United States. After December 31, Belgium, Colombia and Syria were elected to replace Egypt, the Netherlands and Mexico. The Canadian representative on the commission has been, and is, General A. G. L. McNaughton.
At the outset, the atomic energy commission was presented with, two different plans. The United States government at the first meeting of the commission on June 14 put forward proposals for the international control of atomic energy closely resembling in many respects the plan as outlined in the Lilienthal report. The United States government's proposals included the renunciation of the atomic bomb as a weapon and suggested that when an adequate system of control had been established the manufacture of atomic bombs should stop, the existing bombs should be disposed of and the authority set up to administer the system of control should be placed in possession of the technological data necessary for the production of atomic energy. In addition, the United States government's proposals contained a statement which had no counterpart in the Lilienthal report "that there must be no veto to protect those who violate their solemn agreements not to develop or use atomic energy for destructive purposes".
At the second meeting of the commission on June 19, the Soviet government put forward its plan proposing the immediate outlawry of atomic weapons and the destruction of all stocks of atomic energy weapons within a three months' period. In addition, the Soviet government proposed an international convention for the prohibition of the production and use of atomic energy and the establishment of two committees; a "committee for the exchange of scientific information", and a "committee for the prevention of the Use of atomic energy to the detriment of mankind".
Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Egypt, France, Mexico and the United Kingdom agreed in principle that the United States plan might form the basis of discussion in the commission. The Polish and Soviet representatives considered the Soviet plan should be given equal consideration with the proposals advanced by the United States government.
In June and July four committees were established by the commission: a working committee or a committee of the whole; a committee described' as No. 2; a legal and advisory committee; and a scientific and technical committee.
The discussions which ensued occupied the attention of the commission until July 31, at which time the commission went into committee to discuss in detail the question of whether an effective control of atomic energy was possible. The scientific and technical committee was instructed to report its findings with an indication of the methods by which it believed control might be achieved. In October the committee reported that "they did not find any basis in the available scientific facts for supposing that effective control is not technologically feasible."
The work of the scientific and technical committee coincided with the chairmanship of the Canadian representative from August 14 to September 14. and consequently responsibility for suggesting the next step which might be taken in the work of the commission fell upon the Canadian chairman. The Canadian delegation accordingly put forward a proposal that:
Committee No. 2 proceed to examine and report on the safeguards required at eacli stage in the production and use of atomic energy for peaceful purposes, to prevent the possibilities of misuse indicated in the report of the scientific and technical committee; that the committee may hold informal meetings as it may decide, at which scientific representatives may take part in the discussions.
The informal discussions which ensued proved of value in clarifying both the nature and the degree of the control which it is necessary to apply. In the discussions on raw materials the Canadian delegation was able to make a useful contribution by having officials from the bureau of mines and from the Eldorado refinery describe the characteristics of the processes of mining and refining of uranium.
In November it was proposed that the commission should report its proceedings, findings and recommendations to the security council in a first report by December 31. It was agreed that prior to this, committee No. 2 should report to the commission in plenary session. This proposal was accepted by the majority of the commission with the Soviet representative reserving the position of his government and the Netherlands and French representatives accepting on the "understanding that the
Atomic Energy Commission

report would merely record the progress made in the commission to the end of the year without affecting the discussions in the commission."
At a further plenary session of the commission on December 5 the United States delegate introduced proposals for the inclusion of certain items in the findings and recommendations of the commission's report to the security council. These proposals cover some of the main elements of the United States plan as submitted on June 14.
During this time the general assembly of the united nations meeting in New York was debating the subject of disarmament, not only in relation to armed forces and their armament generally, but also specifically to the major weapons adaptable to mass destruction, including atomic weapons.
At a meeting of the commission on December 20. the Canadian delegation put forward a resolution which reads as follows:
Resolved that the commission approves and accepts the principles on which the findings and recommendations proposed by the representatives of the United States of America are based and instructs the working committee to include these findings and recommendations in the draft of the commission's report to be delivered to the security council by the 31st December, 1946, having conformed the wording of such portions of these findings and recommendations as deal with the same subject matter to the wording of the relevant parts of the text of general assembly resolution of December 14, 1946, on the "Principles Governing the General Regulation and Reduction of Armaments."
The Canadian resolution was adopted by the commission by a vote of 10 to 0 and accordingly the proposals as contained in the findings and recommendations of the first report of the atomic energy commission to the security council were amended. The first report of the atomic energy commission was subsequently approved and adopted for transmission to the security council on December 31 by a vote of 10 to 0. with the Soviet and Polish representatives abstaining. That is the report I have tabled today.
In January and February the security council discussed the commission's report at a number of meetings in which the Canadian representative. General McNaughton, participated under the provisions of article 31 of the charter of the united nations. Important statements of the positions of the Soviet and United States governments were made by their representatives on the security council. It became clear that, while all the members of the council were agreed on certain of the proposals, there was disagreement on a number of other proposals. including those on international inspec-

tion and on sanctions. It was clearly impossible to attempt to reconcile these differences in the security council and the council, therefore, decided to refer the matter back to the atomic energy commission. The atomic energy commission has been instructed by the council to prepare and submit to the council a draft treaty or treaties, or convention or conventions incorporating its ultimate proposals. In addition, the security council has requested the commission to submit a second report to the security council before the next session of the general assembly-that which will take place in September, 1947.
Because the discussion has been in general terms, there has been a good deal of misunderstanding about the position, for example, of the United States government on the question of sanctions against violators of an international treaty on the control of atomic energy. The latest statement of the United States representative on this subject has done much to clear up these obscurities. In an address on March 4 before the Overseas Press Club in New York, Mr. Austin, the United States representative on the security council and on the atomic energy commission, had this to say about the vexed question of the veto:
Nothing could be more dangerous than to act upon the assumption that a treaty or a voting system would operate automatically.
Let me illustrate the point by a brief reference to the veto. The veto power in the security council is widely thought of as a protection to an aggressor nation. Actually the veto would be no protection at all to an aggressor if the other nations should act together in accordance with the purposes and principles of the charter.
If any great nation possessing the veto power should ever embark on a course of aggression in violation of the charter, it would be committing an act of nullification, an act of rebellion against the united nations. It would forfeit its position under the charter.
No veto could protect such a nation from the consequences of its crime. Only the failure of the other nations to act together against it could spare the aggressor from lawful punishment. The heart of the problem of building collective security is the strength and the will of the member nations to carry out their obligations, individually and collectively.
Veto or no veto, the strength of the great nations in relation to one another is such that no one of them can safely go to war in violation of the charter if it is certain that the others would act together in the defence of the charter.
If the United States demonstrates convincingly that all its great material and moral power would be used in support of collective security under the united nations, that fact would have far-reaching influence upon the will and capacity of other member nations to act together to maintain peace. On the other hand, if we should falter, if we should dissipate our strength, if we should act in blind or shortsighted selfishness, we would inevitably undermine the whole cause.

Atomic Energy Commission
On March 10, Mr. Austin, speaking as the United States representative on the security council, in answering the Soviet representative's criticism of the United States government's position, said what the United States and the majority of the members of the commission were seeking was-and these are his words-"effective international control by a genuinely international cooperative development of atomic energy to which all nations would contribute their skills and their knowledge without secrecy, and in which all nations would share the benefits on an equitable basis. Our purpose is to assure that each nation can safely realize these tremendous benefits for itself without danger to its national security or the security of its own economic and social system." Mr. Austin went on to say: "The United States does not desire to impose its will, in questions of atomic energy, on other countries. The report itself proves the opposite. Ten countries united therein to forestall an atomic weapons race. The prohibition of atomic weapons in advance of a system of effective enforceable safeguards would not fulfil the mandate of the general assembly adopted unanimously, or prevent an atomic weapons race. My government has made it clear that we welcome all constructive suggestions which might advance the solution of our common problem and fulfil the mandate of the general assembly resolution."
It is to be expected that the studies in the atomic energy commission during the next four or five months will indicate precisely the safeguards which wall be required to protect complying states against the hazards of violations and evasions of the ultimate international agreement on the control of atomic energy. As is stated in the introductory paragraph to section C of the report which I am tabling today, the commission hitherto has limited its examination of the problems of safeguards and measures of control "to the more technical aspects of the control of atomic energy".
It is the hope of the Canadian government that further examination by the atomic energy commission of the problems placed before it by the general assembly of the united nations may lead to a realization on the part of all governments represented on the commission of the manifest advantages to be reaped under a system of effective control of atomic energy. The establishment of such a system would not only make a great contribution to the peace of the world, but would also make it possible for the peoples of the whole world to share in the benefits to be derived from the peaceful application of atomic energy. Canada, as a
member of the commission, will continue to do its utmost to resolve the difficulties which still confront the commission.
1 shall keep the house informed, as occasion offers, of the developments in the work of the atomic energy commission, bearing in mind that the results of the work of this commission, when available in the form of a draft treaty or convention, will naturally be submitted to this house for its approval and for the usual procedures of ratification. The present report is an interim report only and the security council in dealing with it recognizes specifically that "final acceptance of any part of the report by any nation is conditioned upon its acceptance of all parts of the control plan in its final form."
There is no commitment until commitment to the treaty in its final form, and that can be made only by bringing the treaty to the houses of parliament for the usual processes of ratification. The ultimate treaty or convention should be one which governments of democratic states can readily commend to their parliaments and peoples for acceptance. It is hoped therefore that the treaty or convention will be accompanied by a full report from the atomic energy commission setting out in detail the arguments and considerations in support of the provisions contained in the treaty or convention. It is also hoped that in the work of the commission a due perspective is maintained, so that the system of international control which is submitted to the nations for approval, goes as far as it is necessary in the matter of controls to provide international security and the benefits to be derived from the peaceful applications of atomic energy, but goes no farther.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DISCONTINUANCE AS OP MARCH 27
speechtext:
I wish to announce that, effective tomorrow, the coupon rationing of meat will be discontinued.
The rationing of any commodity at the consumer level is a difficult and expensive operation. This is so both from the point of view of government administration and also in light of the burden which must necessarily be imposed upon the retail trade and consumer in the handling of coupons, and other routine requirements of the system. The difficulties

have been increased in recent months because the wartime prices and trade board has not been able to retain the experienced staff which was recruited originally under the stimulus of
a wartime emergency.
In the circumstances, the government has decided on a modification of control in this field which we believe will enable the system of coupon rationing, at the consumer level, to be abandoned, but will provide an alternative method which should not reduce exports of meat from Canada, particularly to the United Kingdom where food shortages are still acute.
By order of the wartime prices and trade board, existing regulations in regard to meatless days in public eating places will continue in force. Furthermore, in collaboration with the meat board, the wartime prices and trade board will continue an area distribution of meat in an effort to ensure an equitable distribution of the available meat supply to specified domestic areas. An effort will be made to hold the supplies going to each area at a level which will not reduce the amount of meat which would have been available for export if the rationing system had continued. Naturally this may not work out exactly. It will require the full cooperation of the public to prevent the supplies for each area from being too rapidly exhausted, thereby causing spotty or temporary shortages. With this in mind, the government will undertake certain publicity measures to inform the public of the need for restraint in this regard, and to invite their cooperation so as to keep this country's export contributions of meat at the highest level possible.

MAXIMUM LOADING ORDER AND PENALTY DEMURRAGE
speechtext:
On March 9, as reported on
page 1512 of Hansard, I replied orally to the following question asked by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher):
1.	11 ave the railroads filed with the board of transport commissioners an application to incorporate emergency orders T.C. order 04F (maximum loading order) and T.C. order 18F (penalty demurrage), in tariff CFA, No. 67?
2.	Was this tariff an emergency order that came into being as a wartime measure?
3.	Has the board of transport commissioners taken any action to make this measure permanent?
My reply was as follows:
I think I can reply orally to this question by telling the hon. gentleman that the railway association of Canada have filed with the board of transport commissioners an application such as is mentioned in the first part of the question to continue the emergency orders of the transport controller. In view of the extension which was given yesterday to the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act 1945 until May 15. the transport controller will continue to exercise jurisdiction over these orders during this extension.
After conferring with the Minister of Justice, I find that order in council P.C. 4487 of June 9, 1942, under which all orders of the transport controller were made, will not be included in the bill called the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, and that this order in council and regulations made thereunder will be revoked in the general revocation of orders and regulations of the governor in council which the government proposes to make effective the first day of April, 1947. Consequently I wish to correct any impression which hon. members may have received from my statement of March 19 that the orders of the transport controller would continue beyond April 1, and to make the following supplementary answer to the hon. member's question.
1.	The Railway Association of Canada has filed with the board of transport commissioners an application requesting the issuance of a general order of the board which would have the effect of continuing, after the cessation of the transport controller's authority, the provisions of emergency orders T.C. 04-F, 05-F and 18-F incorporated in tariff CFA No. 67.
2.	Tariff CFA No. 67, which is based on said orders T.C. 04-F, 05-F and 18-F, has not yet been approved by the board and is not in force.
3.	The board of transport commissioners has not yet dealt with the said application of the railway association but I expect will do so in the near future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the orders
of the day yesterday the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) referred to a statement made in the British House of Commons on Monday of this week by Sir Stafford Cripps on the subject of the British preferential tariff. The hon. member has asked me to make a preliminary statement to this house on the same subject.
In Hansard of March 17 last, at page 1415, my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) set forth at some length the position on the British preferential tariff shared by the British and Canadian governments having regard to approaching negotiations at the second part of the world trade conference, opening in Geneva on April 10.
This general declaration of policy is fully in line with the address I made to the Canadian Manufacturers Association, Ottawa Valley branch, on April 10, 1946, a copy of which the hon. member for Danforth very kindly sent over to me yesterday. I shall quote one paragraph from the statement I made at that time:
The proposals to be considered by the world trade conference, I would like to emphasize, make it quite clear that all tariff changes are to be made on an agreed international basis. There is no question of any nation or group of nations being asked to make tariff reductions which will not be matched by tariff concessions from all the member countries.
I know the historic contribution made by the system of imperial preference to the growth and expansion of our commerce. I am also ready to agree that this is not simply a question of trade, but is an issue which may affect the larger question of our relations in the British family of nations. Let me therefore emphasize as strongly as I can that Great Britain and Canada and the United States are all agreed that the one thing which has been decided upon is the procedure to be folio-wed at the conference. There is no intention to abolish imperial preferences, or to agree to large reductions in imperial preferences in exchange for meagre or nominal reductions in the tariff of the United States and other countries.
What was said on Monday last in the British House of Commons by Sir Stafford Cripps does not, it appeal's to me, add to or subtract from this government's attitude on this subject.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext:
Before the order of the day is called may I say a word on the matter of procedure on a resolution preceding a money bill. I have had occasion to refer to this matter of procedure each session because of the length of time that has been consumed in discussion when similar resolutions have been considered to an extent and in a manner which is entirely contrary to the rules. I am referring at the moment to what it would seem may come to be possibly the case with respect to the discussion in committee on the resolution which will be called as the first order. It always seems that the government may be taking the point of view it does because of some particular measure that is before the house. It is not that. I am raising the point at the moment in order that hon. members may follow the rules of the house which have been framed in the interests of all hon. members.
Last year, with respect to a loan being made to the United Kingdom, I spoke in

regard to the procedure in committee on the resolution preceding a money bill. With the permission of the house I should like to read a paragraph from what I said at that time with a view to pointing out that- it applies equally to any aud every measure of a similar character. The statement I made wull be found in Hansard of April, 19-16, at page 761:
The rule is that a resolution must precede a money bill, but the resolution is intended merely as a notice to the house that a money bill is about to be introduced. It is not intended that the notice should be debatable; rather, the correct practice is that the resolution should be allowed to pass, the house go into committee and that, in committee, a statement be_ made on essential features of the bill which is later to be introduced, this to follow if so desired by some brief discussion. It is not intended that a lengthy discussion should take place at that stage. The discussion on the bill should come after the bill itself is introduced.
That statement is entirely in accordance with the rules of the house. It was made, as hon. members will see, in relation to the bill in respect to the loan to Britain at the last session, but it applies equally to the bill which is before us at the present time.
I hold in my hand a copy of Sir Thomas Erskine May's parliamentary procedure, fourteenth edition, as edited by Sir Gilbert Campion, who is the recognized authority on parliamentary procedure. At page 732 hon. members will find the following statement with reference to the scope of debate on resolution:
Debate in committee on a financial resolution is confined to the terms of the resolution itself and must not be extended to the related bill.
These are the words to which I wish to draw hon. members' attention. As I looked over the debate yesterday I observed that a good many questions did relate specifically to the bill that is based on the resolution. It is quite contrary to parliamentary practice that the discussion in committee on the resolution should be extended to the related bill. I mention this simply because among other things, the length of time this session is likely to run is going to be very considerable unless we all observe strictly the rules of the house.
If we had observed the rule with respect to the introduction of the resolution itself and passed it in a formal manner we should have saved a week of discussion already. There has been a week of discussion on the resolution. Practically all of that discussion will be repeated when we come to the bill itself. If the house is to take an indefinite time in debate in the committee on the resolution there is no saying when the house will be able to get through the work of the present session.
Let me mention to hon. members that if, through discussion on this particular measure,

Business of the House
we run on to the end of April, three months of the session will have passed. There will remain practically all the business of the session still to complete. That will mean that at the end of April we shall up to that time have had no opportunity to discuss the budget; we shall not have had opportunity to discuss any of the estimates; we shall not have time for any of the ordinary legislation of the session. By the time we get on into the spring hon. members I am sure will be hoping that we shall not continue during the summer into the autumn. That is a consequence which must follow unless we do in some way seek to curtail unnecessary discussion. I do not wish to curtail anyone contrary to the rules. I do not want to suggest that there should not be the fullest and freest discussion. All I am asking is that hon. members shall follow the rules as they are set forth in the rules of the house. If the rules are not adequate, let us change them. So long as they are there, let us follow them.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext: May I be permitted to comment on the Prime Minister's statement? There is no desire, as I think the Prime Minister will realize, on the part of our party to delay in any way the proceedings in connection with the matter-

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext: I hope that kind of thing is not organized by the government. I wTish to say to the Prime Minister that at the beginning of the resolution stage my leader made it very clear that this party was prepared to allow the resolution to go through on the basis that when we reached the committee stage there would be full opportunity on the part of opposition parties and others to examine the ministry, to ask and receive answers to questions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext: The committee stage on the resolution or the committee stage on the bill?

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext:
The committee stage on the resolution. I am not complaining about the leader of the C.C.F., although immediately afterwards he made a speech which raised many questions, and of course it could not be allowed to go unchallenged. I am careful not to hold him or anyone else responsible, because everyone in the bouse must take his own responsibility. I do not think, however, that this is the kind of bill that the Prime Minister had in mind when he was reading the opinions he had. This is not an ordinary bill. It is not really one bill but fifty-seven bills, and it is impossible to apply even custom, let alone
the rules, to a bill in which there are fifty-seven units. The house is struggling to get information on the legislation as speedily as possible, having in mind the relation of dispatch to the public interest in general.
The Prime Minister has said that normally the minister in charge of the bill should make a statement on the resolution setting forth the essential features of the measure. But there are fifty-seven essential features to this resolution. While the Prime Minister has had long experience in matters of this kind, I still think it really gets down to the question of how a matter of this kind should be dealt with. That is a matter of opinion and I think the circumstances in which we now find ourselves will have to dictate the time that may be taken. I have not had nearly as long an experience as the Prime Minister, but I suggest that most members feel that not much time is wasted in dealing with a matter at one stage rather than another, because what members have to say at one time will seldom be repeated at another stage of the proceedings.
I beg your pardon. Mr. Speaker, for having taken so much time, but I felt called upon to answer the Prime Minister, because I am afraid that what he has said cannot meet with full agreement on this side.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext:
May I add this? I believe I was responsible for the initiation of the debate last Thursday evening. Looking at Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms I find this:
Minister moves that Speaker leave the Chair for house to go into committee of the whole on the resolution. Speaker puts question on motion. (Debate allowed.)
It may be that the Prime Minister is quite right that this procedure does prolong the consideration of a particular matter. A few moments ago he quoted from another authority. Sometimes we find that one authority is cited in this house for a particular procedure, and sometimes, another. But our own authority-I looked it up beforehand, I may say-does clearly state, though the rule may not be a good one, that the minister moves that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of the whole on the resolution; the Speaker puts the motion, and debate is allowed.
That is why we began the debate last Thursday evening. If you turn to page 159 and look at 418, in the second paragraph you will find:
The ordinary function of a committee of the whole house is deliberation, not inquiry. All matters concerning the imposition of taxes, or the grant of public money, must be considered in committee, as a preliminary to legislation;
Business of the House

and any other questions which, in the opinion of the house, may be more fitly discussed in committee, are dealt with in that manner. The provisions of public bills are usually considered in a committee of the whole house.
It was on our own book of rules, Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, that we based both the speech and the amendment we moved last Thursday evening.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I enjoy listening to the Prime Minister, who has such wide experience in parliamentary matters, but he spoke about debating resolutions of this kind, and if I am not mistaken he said that the discussion should not be on the related bill. How could it be? We have not got it. I do not think we have the bill now, and therefore, as we have not the bill, we do not know what is in it and it is pretty difficult to discuss the bill itself.
There is a distinction between the procedure in England and procedure here. Naturally we have some of the principles of British rules, but we have custom according to our pattern, and the result is an entirely different stew. In the parliament at Westminster the purpose of the resolution on a money bill is to notify the members that the government has obtained royal assent to sponsoring a certain bill, and the purpose of the discussion-not the debate, mark you, sir, but the discussion of the resolution in the committee-is precisely to afford the opportunity to members of parliament to ask questions of the ministry and also to make suggestions in order to improve the bill with their own experience. This we may call debating, if we wish; but at the present time I presume that the bill is all cooked and is kept in the icebox of the Department of Justice and will be served to us on a silver platter a little later, as soon as we are through with this resolution. Therefore debating this resolution means positively nothing, because whatever bombshell we may find in the resolution will not affect the bill even if it explodes.
There is something more than the big book that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has quoted from. There is a very small book called Standing Orders of the House of Commons, 1936. One day a member of parliament of ten years' experience asked me, "What do they mean by standing orders?" I said, "They are the regulations of the house, the rules of the house." I have the standing orders in my hand, and at page 17, rule 38, paragraph 1, I read:
38. (1) The following motions are debatable:
Every motion
(a) standing on the order of proceedings for the day (except government notices of motion for the house to go into committee at a later date);

This motion is on the order of proceedings for the day and therefore it is debatable. I am the more at ease in making these remarks, in all humility and candour, for the reason that I have not spoken on the resolution since it has been before the committee. But I am interested in getting some information; there is no man on earth who will prevent me from asking for it, and I will stand up again and again until I get it, because I want to be informed, even if the bill is cooked and is in the refrigerator of the Department of Justice. I want to get some information about this resolution. The denial of that right is antidemocratic, and I am sure the Prime Minister will not insist upon it. I am just as anxious as he is to get rid of the session and go home, although I enjoy the company of my colleagues. I find that my part of the country is the finest in the land; it is God's country, but I am here to do my duty. It is a great sacrifice for me to stay here, and my reward will be to get the information I ask for every time I ask for it. I am sure the Prime Minister is too fair-minded to insist otherwise. Therefore we must take with a grain of salt everything that is said regarding the interpretation of the rules. Campion is a famous author. For a long time he was assistant clerk at Westminster, and if I am not mistaken he is the clerk now. I know he is a great man; I know his book, but to quote from that book as against a standing order which is our rule of debate in this house- I do not say our rule of discussion, but our rule of debate-is not fair. We cannot quote Campion against rule 38, paragraph 1.
Therefore, sir, I suggest., not for your benefit but for the benefit of hon. members who were interested in that debate-because you are in the chair and it was a debate; when the chairman is in the chair, when the house gets into committee, it is discussion-that our rule is the contrary. The rule means debating. I am sure we shall be treated fairly in the future as we have been in the past, and we can take it that when we ask questions it is not done to delay proceedings but to satisfy our minds and get the information we think is in the public interest.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE ON RESOLUTION PRECEDING MONEY BILL
speechtext:
My purpose in rising was to try to prevent two debates where one should suffice. It seems that I have succeeded only in provoking a third debate. However, I should like to say just this word to the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), who referred to Beauchesne, or to his own experiences in the house as to the rules and as to what is permitted or involved in following them. In my hand I have what I might speak of as Beauchesne up to date. Before coming into the house this afternoon I rather expected someone on the opposite side would quote Beauchesne as against what I might wish to say, so I asked the Clerk of the House if he would give me a statement on this point which I could read to the house as authoritative. The statement given me is as follows:
The adoption of the resolution is merely a formal matter and it is often allowed to pass without discussion. The stages of procedure where the principle involved and the details of the measure may be discussed are the second reading of the bill, committee and third reading. When this rule is not applied there is always a repetition of debate.
A moment ago my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition said his experience had shown him there was not much repetition. Well, the Clerk of the House has had a very long experience and close observation of these matters and he says when the rule is not applied there is always a repetition of
debate, and I think that has been the experience of everyone. My purpose is none other than that of trying to economize the time of the house in having its rules obeyed. I cannot agree that because there are some fifty-seven orders in council attached to this bill, therefore the bill is not in the regular form. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) answered that question completely and satisfactorily in what he just said. Really there is in fact less justification or reason for asking questions in committee in connection with this resolution than is frequently the case, since, as the Minister of Justice has just said, these orders in council concerning which questions are being asked have been the law of the land right along for some time and should be and are known to every member of the house. All that is essential in the committee stage on the resolution is a general statement or statements in regard to what is of special significance in the bill based on the resolution. As to this bill, hon. members know much more about what it contains and involves than in the case of most other legislation. So I would submit again that if we wish to get through with the business of the house in a way that will accommodate hon. members most satisfactorily in the end we shall best do so by observing the rules of the house.

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war and to provide therein that the governor in council may appoint and fix the compensation of the officers, clerks and employees necessary for the administration of any order or regulation continued in force by the act and further to provide that certain officers, clerks and employees may continue to perform the duties for which they were previously appointed.

I wanted to know if he would foe good enough to tell us if in this computation of six per cent 'had been included all subsidies, all bonuses, all remissions of duties, all remissions of excise, and other sundry sources of revenue which are denied to the crown by reason of the alleged emergency.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to ask just
one question of the minister, but it is a twofold question. He may not have the information before him now but it should be easy for him to get it. In order to be able to discuss sensibly, not only the resolution but the bill, we should know what commodities are now affected by controls. I am not asking for information about the orders in council because they have been published in book form, but I want the minister and the committee to understand just what I wish to know.
There are a certain number of commodities such as butter, shoes, sugar, milk, hats, ladies' wear, et cetera, which have been rationed or which have been under control. I should like to know why these commodities have been placed under the controls. Certain controls have been lifted while others are still in force. I should like to know why certain controls have been lifted and why other controls have been kept in force. There should be a tabulation to indicate, on the one hand, why controls have been imposed and, on the other hand, why other controls have been lifted. It seems to me that that information is necessary if we are to understand the working of the controls.
I presume it will be impossible for the minister to supply this information now but it should be easily prepared and available tomorrow or on Friday. Then hon. members will know exactly what commodities are under controls at the present time, what commodities are not under controls and what was the reason for the imposition of the controls. I have been informed by some of my friends that the reason why such a large number of hon. members voted in favour of the resolution yesterday was the requirement that a special permit is necessary before a new business can be started and that trusts and cartels and others do not want any new businesses. Apparently that was one reason why such a large number of hon. members voted for the controls.
I was told also by reliable people that another reason for the large vote was the fact that retail, wholesale and manufacturers' prices are established and that some people who are close to the strings may pull them so as to keep the controls in force. That is

Emergency Powers

not my opinion; it is just a rumour which has spread quite widely. Perhaps I could go a little farther in explaining my question because it is a serious question. I received one of the greatest honours I have ever received when the non. member for High Park asked one of my questions the other day.	_
The argument in favour of price controls is that they are imposed to prevent the exploitation of the people, but I submit that the people are not being protected as they should be when the controls are lifted and even when they are still in force. I have not a complete list of the articles that are offered for sale, but from what has been said to me by big businessmen, during the war shoes were classified on the basis of samples which were submitted to the board by the manufacturers. These manufacturers used rubber and other material of a minor quality to make up the samples. The shoes were not as good but they were sold either at the same price or at higher prices.
Last year there was an increase in the price of agricultural implements. This came as a bolt from the blue. It was a surprise to all of us. It was announced by my right hon. friend the minister apparently as a matter of routine. Not a word was said to me about it, but I know that some of his colleagues looked surprised when the announcement was made in the house. It was decided that agricultural implements would sell at a higher price than before. There are all sorts of things like this that should be investigated. Does my right hon. friend think a pair of shoes is worth $16? Does he think a hat made from material costing $1, or perhaps only fifty cents, with from twenty-five to fifty cents worth of work on it, should sell for $15, $25 or $30?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is the idea.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The idea is to exploit the people. If it was known that the people were being exploited, how is it that the prices board ignored that fact? I understand that is why some controls are lifted, to please a certain class of individuals, but the exploitation is that of the people.
What about shirts? Is it possible to buy a good shirt today for less than five or six dollars? And the price is rising. The information that was given to me by a man of considerable experience and by others, was that the shirts that we are now paying five dollars for are not worth more than a dollar and a half or two dollars. There is exploitation. If price control exists and is now in force the control must be incompetent. If price control has been lifted from these goods, the price

control board is equally incompetent because it does not impose controls on things which should be controlled.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What about baby diapers?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I spoke of them a long time ago, and the authorities did not know that flannelette was used for that purpose. They thought it was used only for nightshirts. I gave an interview to the press on that, and I have it upstairs.
The ambition of the working man who makes a pair of shoes or a shirt or a suit of clothes is to have enough wages to be able to buy what he makes. That is a natural feeling. But when there are middlemen who make an undue profit at the expense of the masses of the people by overcharging them, that should be stopped, and it is the duty of the government to tell the prices board definitely to stop those practices which make the common people lose all faith in our democratic system.
Is it possible today to buy a shirt of average quality for less than $5? It is impossible, and the shirt that we pay five or six dollars for is not worth any more than two dollars and a half. Why is that? Is there any man who will say that, even if we have a slight touch of inflation, it is reasonable to pay $16 for a pair of shoes? You can go into a store and you will see shoes marked at from twelve to sixteen dollars, and the shoes are not worth more than three or four dollars. Where does the difference go? Not only that but it is very hard to get a suit of clothes. The other day I met a colleague of mine in the house. He was very well attired and I said, "This is a new suit you have on?" He said, "Yes". I said, "You look very well in it," and he said, "Well, I must because I paid $120 for it." That is a considerable sum of money, and there is no interference from the prices board.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Was it worth $50 before 1939?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am not a tailor but I know that before 1939 one could buy a first class suit for $45. If prices had doubled in the interval, that would be only $90 today. But that is how it goes all along the line, and the answer we have from the prices board is that they are protecting us.
Take chocolates, for instance. You go into one store and pay seventy cents a pound for a box of chocolates. Go into another store and you will pay $1 a pound, and in another store you will pay $1.25. How is it there are different prices like that for ordinary chocolates? It reminds me of a trip I made to the Magdalen islands some time ago. I was a young boy and I went into a store which had three different kinds of chocolates. One kind

Emergency Powers
was twenty-five cents a pound; another kind, fifty cents a pound, and the third kind, seventy-five cents a pound. I was young; I was earning my first money, and I asked the storekeeper for some chocolates. The man sold me chocolates for twenty-five cents a pound, 'but that was a favour he was doing me. 1 said, "That is a very reasonable price," and he said, "Yes, but if you were a married man and you came in here with your wife wanting chocolates I would sell you fifty-cent chocolates. That is a little better than the ones we sell to children and a little less extravagant than the ones we sell to boys who call with their sweethearts." The price for children was twenty-five cents; for married men, fifty cents; for bo3rs with their sweethearts, seventy-five cents-all for the same thing.
Mr. CASTLF.DEN: That is private enterprise for you.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No. It was private enterprise uncontrolled by individual honesty. If there were more honesty in business I believe that the number of those who advocate control would be much smaller.
I wish to pay a special tribute to my hon. friend the member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) for the excellent speech he made last week. He also spoke very well this week. He is a man of wide experience, and I am ready to support him in many of the things he said. He told me that there are people, even outside Canada, who go into a store to buy a definite thing costing such-and-such a price and if the article is marked for sale at a cheaper price they will not buy it. They judge the quality by the price, and naturally the merchants cater to their stupidity. We cannot prevent that; it is only human. But the public at large should be protected, and the necessary measures should be taken in order to protect those who go to buy anything so that no one will take advantage of their good faith or of their credulity.
May I say to the minister that I have made these remarks in the best possible spirit, so that if we are to have controls we shall have controls that really help. I am against the form of control that wTe have now because all or most of those who are in control are infallible; what they decide is the word of gospel; they accept no suggestions for changing anything from anybody. Their word is final. I should like to have the same recipe as they have, as those who succeeded in getting an increase in the price of agricultural implements. I should like to have their recipe for adjusting certain prices. Having said that, I hope something will be 83166-1131
done for the betterment of present conditions so that the people will not continue to be exploited as they are. We are exploited; everyone is exploited. Take, for instance, the grain companies. They have an organization to sell flour; they have subsidiaries to sell bread and pastry. They sell pastry at a profit of 400 per cent. They may make lots of profit but there are others who cannot make any. It is not fair, and the people are exploited.
Some years before the war I read an article which was published in a magazine showing the exploitation of the people of the United States in the sale of drug store items. It was formidable. The items consisted of things that are in daily use in- the home and they were sold at an extraordinary profit, an abnormal profit. All that should be corrected if we have an organization to see to it. Perhaps there are better systems than that. They may be explained sooner or later. I am sure that hon. members will give the minister their suggestions for improving conditions that are bad, and at the same time they may say what is good in the whole system. I am sure it will work well only when it is under the direct responsibility of the minister, at the same time the minister being responsible to parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member asked a few questions which I think I can answer now. He asked why certain goods were subject to rationing. I gathered from the nature of the goods he mentioned that he did not mean coupon rationing; he meant why they were subject to orders providing for their equitable distribution. I do not know whether there are outstanding orders in any number providing for the equitable distribution of goods at the present time, but there was a time when there were many orders providing for the equitable distribution of goods.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can we have that information at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, I can get that. The reason for the orders, of course, was the shortage of the goods. When there were not enough goods to supply the trade and the public, the board provided for their equitable distribution.
With regard to rationing in the ordinary sense, there are just two articles subject to rationing since the announcement of the Minister of Finance this afternoon. The two remaining articles are butter and sugar. The reason there is the same one that I gave for the orders for equitable distribution, namely, that the demand is greater than the supply

The hon. member asked me to give the committee the names of articles that are controlled. In one sense the prices of all goods and services are subject to control, because one section of the wartime prices and trade board order starts with these words:
That no person shall sell or offer for sale or supply any goods or services at a price that is higher than is reasonable and just or withhold any goods or services from sale or supply for a price that is higher than is reasonable and just.
It will be apparent that that provision is an extraordinarily difficult one to enforce. The reliance for enforcement must be based mainly on ceilings.
Perhaps the hon. member meant to ask me what articles are still subject to ceilings. Nearly all goods and services were at one time subject to ceilings, but in the summer of 1946 I made a statement in the house in which I said that thereafter only those goods and services which were named in the statement would be subject to ceilings and that others would be free from the control of ceiling prices. The control there would simply have to be the control that is found in the provision I have read, namely, that the prices of these must be not greater than what is reasonable and just. I have not that list before me, nor is it material, because in January the present Minister of Finance made an additional statement. His additional statement is found at page 67 of the report of the wartime prices and trade board. At that time the list of goods and services remaining subject to maximum prices was reduced. The list is still a long one. That list, in condensed form, but nevertheless complete, was published in the papers last January. It is a long list of classes of goods and services rather than of specific goods and services. I have before me the notice which was published in the paper, but of course it is so long that it would be difficult for me to incorporate it in my present remarks. I am informed by the officer of the wartime prices and trade board that probably seventy or seventy-five per cent in volume of all goods are still subject to ceiling prices, although great numbers of categories have been released from the control of ceiling prices.
The hon. member asked the reasons for removing ceilings, for removing articles from control. These reasons were set out in the statement made by the Minister of Finance on January 11, and the part of the statement enumerating these reasons is found on page 68 of the report of the wartime prices and trade board.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: For the year 1946?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The 1946 report. The statement was made on January 11, 1947, and it is in the 1946 report. The Minister of Finance said:
There are a number of reasons behind the choice of these items for release from price control.
Improvement in supplies. When supplies are good, and particularly when they are sufficiently ample to produce prices below established ceilings, as in the case of a number of fresh vegetables, there is every reason for decontrol. When supplies of goods which are not fully adequate show every sign of improving further and when competition is increasing, as in the case of many household articles, there is also strong reason to remove price control. When competition in world markets is becoming keener and supplies are fairly satisfactory, as is generally the situation with fish, removal of price control is justified, though in some cases it remains necessary to maintain control over the quantity of exports to assure sufficient supplies in the domestic market.
Administrative problems. The burden, expense and complexity of administration when viewed against the lessening risk of serious price advances threw the balance toward decontrol in some fields. To an increasing extent, the relationship of prices as between standard and new lines in some businesses appeared to be having the effect of encouraging the production of new lines at the expense of output in lower-priced standard lines. This problem existed in regard to furniture and some household utensils and could not, at this stage, be entirely met under the general price control policy. Then again, there were a number of fields in which necessary price adjustments were pending. When this was the case and when it was believed that competition was growing and consumer resistance likely to develop in any event, decontrols seemed to be the best course.
There was also the risk that ceiling prices might come to be regarded as minimum prices- as the prices which the government authorized sellers to charge. Accordingly, in some cases where the threat of sharp price increases was passing, the government "was disposed to withdraw from price control and to let the trade consider its own longer-range position without any suggestion of government intervention.
In the case of some imports such as tapioca, arrowroot, and peanuts, it was necessary to choose between alternatives of letting the going ivorld price be reflected in Canada, of maintaining ceilings by payment of substantial subsidies, or of going without such imported commodities. In these circumstances, the course of decontrol was chosen.
That constitutes a fairly complete statement of the reasons for decontrolling any particular article or class of articles. I am unable to deal with the specific commodities mentioned by my hon. friend, but one can imagine the difficulty of effective price control of articles such as women's hats, because it is not possible to relate them to the prices charged for the same kind of hat in the fall of 1941 when there was not the same type of hat. With the passage of time, the ceiling

Emergency Powers
principle becomes more and more difficult to apply to the control of prices of certain goods. The same considerations apply to many other commodities. It is impossible in price control to do a scientifically complete or perfect job. There will be some undue profits, no matter how competent the officials may be. They can only do their best.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wish to ask a question regarding the government's general policy on subsidies. I understand that during the war the government's justification for the payment of subsidies lay in the fact that they considered that the saving to the consumer would be greater than the cost of taxation, owing partly to the danger from a spiral of inflation. I think that is generally correct, and the spiral of inflation would not be due so much to the expansion of money but would be due to the fact that, although there had. been a tre1-mendous increase in production, somewhere in the neighbourhood of fifty per cent of that production was drained away from the channels of consumption for war purposes, and therefore the money paid out on that production would, become a demand against consumption goods left in the country; that is, generally speaking. Then, coming to peace time, I understand the government's attitude toward subsidies is this, that they do not consider they would be justified in continuing the subsidy at a time when the cost in taxation may become as great as the saving to the consumer from the subsidy. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know that I can state the view of the government in that regard. I should think it would be pretty doubtful whether the' payment of a subsidy is justified when it is simply the transference of purchasing power from one group of Canadian citizens to a slightly different group of Canadian citizens. Other considerations might enter in. It might, as a matter of social policy or something of that kind, be desirable to make that transfer of purchasing power, that redistribution of wealth, but it certainly would not be a policy for the prevention of inflation under these conditions. From the point of view of inflation prevention, it seems to me that when that point is reached subsidies should be abolished, if they are being considered as an anti-inflation device.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
On the other hand, if later on we reach a position such as the governor of the Bank of Canada indicates in the 1946 report, where we may have great difficulty in maintaining demand against our production, then it might be advisable to pay a consumer subsidy in order to expand demand within
Canada. But, as the minister says, if that subsidy is paid from taxation, then the cost in taxation may be as great as the saving to the consumer and therefore you would not be increasing demand. The minister must admit that if that subsidy were paid from some other source than taxation it might be possible to expand demand in relation to production. It might be from idle savings, although, if you have to repay those savings at a later date you will still have the problem of a deficiency of purchasing power to deal with. You could finance the subsidy from the expansion of money through the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think we are getting too far from the resolution. We are getting into the realm of monetary theory.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But the resolution provides for the continuation of orders in council in relation to subsidies, and I was trying to get from the minister what the government's policy was on subsidies in peace time. He agrees that, generally speaking, so far as he himself is concerned-he may not be speaking on behalf of the government-in his opinion the consumer subsidy should stop when the cost in taxation becomes as great as the saving from the subsidy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would have to add the qualification, unless it is desired for another purpose entirely, and I have used the term "social policy"-the redistribution of wealth. A policy of that kind, taking money from some people and giving it to others, might be desirable under certain conditions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would not the cost in taxation always equal the amount of the subsidy? I do not see how it could happen that the cost from the tax with which the subsidy was paid would be more or less than the subsidy itself.

The other point I would ask the minister is this. There might be a great deal of
