speechtext: The subsidies made the control possible. The hon. gentleman is right; prices had to be controlled, too, but if there had been control alone without subsidies over a certain period there would have been no production.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The minister made a considerable point of the fact that the increase in the cost of living in Canada since the war ended had been only six per cent, whereas in the United States, where controls have been abandoned, the cost of living index has risen eighteen per cent. My colleague the hon. member for Stanstead asked the minister whether or not the matter of subsidies, on which we spend a good deal of money each year, was taken into account when the Canadian cost of living index was computed. The minister said it was not, and I believe he went on to say he did not have the figures available. I should like to follow that up with several other matters which I think affect the cost of living index in Canada, and I wish to know whether the minister is able to tell us if these have also been taken into account, or if they have been neglected.
First of all, I refer to the matter of exports. To give a practical example, we find that in the lumber industry of this country we are allowed to export about forty per cent of the total cut, of which a large part goes to the United States where there is no price control on that product. As a result, our mills in Canada receive a great deal more money for this lumber which is exported, and the Canadian price on lumber used in domestic construe-

tion, and in other ways where it enters into the cost of production and therefore the cost of living, is kept down. The proof of this statement lies in the fact that if a producer of one of these commodities, part of whose output is exported, finds that he is not making a satisfactory profit on his domestic sales and applies to the wartime prices and trade board for an increase in price, clearly showing that he is receiving, let us say, $50 per 1,000 board feet for his domestic output and $75 or $80 for his exports, he will be told, "Yes, but your overall profit is satisfactory. Therefore, even if you are losing on your domestic output you are making enough on your exports to give you a fair over-all return." I am not quarreling with that policy, but I wish to point out that our cost of living index is manifestly unfair because we are taking advantage of a free market in the United States, where prices are uncontrolled, in order that in Canada we may quote prices which are substantially below the cost of production. Perhaps the minister will look into this matter-he may have the figures available from the wartime prices and trade board-and tell the committee just how much higher the cost of living would be in this country but for the fact that we take advantage of the free market in the United States and perhaps other countries. Then we may be able to get a true picture of what the cost of living index really would be in this country and whether or not controls have been a good thing for us. I am suggesting that it is unfair for us to sell part of our product in a free market and use the profit in order to show an unfair comparison with prices in our own market.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Unfair to whom?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The comparison is unfair to the Canadian people if you are trying to show what controls have done, because you are taking advantage of an uncontrolled market across the line. I am not saying that is a bad thing for Canada, but a comparison of the costs of living in the two countries is unfair because our cost is artificially lowered by reason of the fact that we are taking advantage of a market where the price is higher as a result of the removal of controls.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But it is lower; the Canadian purchaser does pay less.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes. If the hon. member had been here when I began my remarks he would understand the point I am trying to get at.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was following my hon. friend very closely.

Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In the beginning I said many products were sold in Canada at less than the cost of production because part of the output of the particular factory or mill is sold in a foreign country where prices are uncontrolled, and that therefore our cost of living index has in it an element which is below the cost of production by reason of the fact that we are selling in a free market across the line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is good government in Canada, I would say.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not objecting to that. It may be good government; I am not passing judgment on the policy, but I suggest that it is unfair to compare the cost of living in Canada with the cost of living across the line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the cost of living.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I did not say it was not, but I am suggesting that we are selling many products in this country at less than the cost of production, which is obviously an artificial situation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The Americans are getting value for their money.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member can make his speech later if he wishes.
The next point I desire to make is that I hear it said-and perhaps the minister can confirm my impression or disabuse my mind -that when price increases are asked for by manufacturers or producers they are much more likely to receive favourable consideration, if they have a just case, if the particular product on which they are asking the price increase is not included in the cost of living index. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to furnish the committee with a list of those products on which price increases have been granted, let us say since June 30, 1946, when the OPA went out of existence in the United States, and a list of those products in regard to which applications were made for increases but on which increases were refused, so that we might find out by a quick reference whether or not there is any truth in this assertion which is heard so frequently.
Another point which also affects our cost of living index is the fact that almost immediately after the OPA disappeared in the United 'States, or only five days later, we did away with the differential in our dollar exchange rate with the United States, bringing the Canadian dollar to parity with the currency of that country. I am not complaining just now about that action, but I wish to point out
that there is an element of unfairness in our cost of living index by reason of that change, as compared with the United States index. What actually happened was that it was made ten per cent easier to buy a vast quantity of commodities in the United States because the Canadian dollar was raised to parity in place of a ten per cent discount as compared with the United States dollar. Undoubtedly that had an influence on the price we had to pay in United States dollars for orange juice, citrus fruits and all the great number of commodities we buy in the United States. That had an effect on the cost of living index which, I believe, invalidated it in reference to any comparison with the United States cost of living index. At that time we had an estimated $1,500,060,000 of United States exchange, and the change in the exchange rate cost this country, on paper at least, about $150,000,000, quite a substantial amount and which undoubtedly would have a real effect on the cost of living index.
What I suggest to the minister is that if he could answer these points which I have raised, and perhaps have his department calculate the effect which they otherwise would have had on the cost of living index in Canada, we might find that, in place of our cost of living index not having gone up as much as prices in the United States, despite the continuance of controls in this country and the arguments offered for further continuance, there has not been very much difference between the cost of living here and the cost of living across the border.
The minister has not mentioned the fact that under these price controls we have black markets, the extent of which is perhaps not as widely known to government agents as it is to people in various businesses, where it has been found that legitimate business, from which a reasonable profit is expected, is put out of operation because black marketeers can make large profits and cut into the trade. In fact, some of them are making so much money that they have firmly established themselves, and are likely to be with us, perhaps on a legitimate basis, for many years to come, all to the detriment of the ordinary trade and the ordinary Canadian taxpayer.
Furthermore, while we point to a comparison of the cost of living index here with that in the United States, nothing is said about the control of standards. It is well known by the wartime prices and trade board that, while a price may remain the same on a particular article, the standard of quality may bear no relation whatsoever to the pre-war standard.
Emergency Powers

As a matter of fact, very often these controls are nothing more or less than protection of inefficiency. Some businessmen like them because if they get a fixed price for buying and a fixed price for selling, with an adequate margin, they are content, and would like to see a continuation of that system. On the other hand, one of the greatest virtues of the whole system of free enterprise is that those who are inefficient disappear. If they cannot hold their own and render service to the people at reasonable prices, it is soon found that someone else takes their place and their business. As a matter of fact, when the government asks for the continuation of so many of these controls it should be remembered that during the war years we greatly increased our industrial capacity- perhaps by forty per cent-and managed to keep ourselves supplied. Furthermore, a million of our best young men and women were engaged in war industry, while another 800,000 of our best young people were in the armed services. Of that total of 1,800,000, at least 1,500,000 seem now to be employed, and engaged in turning out goods for peace time, in place of goods for war.
Surely the time has come when we can have competition, and when we can have goods available, if the free system is allowed to have its head and really get going. We had an example when only the other day the Ford Company of Canada reduced the price of its product, voluntarily; because all businessmen, and particularly those who really understand about business-I speak more particularly of the larger concerns-are united in thinking that the last thing they want is to see a run-away market, from which economic chaos would result.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What was the percentage of reduction?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not know what
the percentage of reduction of the Ford Company was, but one of my colleagues tells me it was $35 a car. Meantime, wages have gone up, and the reduction was most creditable.
One almost forgets that our economic system ever got along without controls. We had controls during the war, and many of us appreciate what they did to regulate the economj' of this country, and to do a good job of concentrating our efforts on war production. But the impression is growing up, having been under the tutelage of controls for the last seven or eight years, that we cannot get along without them. We are almost afraid to venture forth into the water for fear of drowning. We have to hang on to a life-preserver, a rope, or something of that kind. Business is

quite capable of taking care of itself. Supply and demand, production and consumption, are quite capable of adjusting themselves so that there will be a fair and equitable and, more particularly, a greater supply of goods than there would be under a controlled system.
I suggest to the minister that if he will give business its head he will find that there will be more production, and that competition will keep prices down. In fact, it is greatly to be questioned whether or not the government is of the opinion that we are heading for inflation or deflation. The consensus of the largest number of economists in North America at the present time is that we are facing at least a moderate price, recession. If that is so, then it means that demand is being overtaken by supply. When that happens there will always be some manufacturers who will want to keep their factories going 100 per cent, with the result that they will lower prices in order to get the business.
I should like very much to hear from the minister whether he or his advisers expect that we are heading for deflation, with perhaps some unemployment connected with it, or whether we are heading for inflation. Certainly if we are heading for deflation it is hardly the time to inaugurate or to put into statutory form the continuation of these controls.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We are not inaugurating it. In putting them into statutory form, we are simply continuing them for as long as is necessary, thereby permitting our getting out of them in an orderly fashion, as I have explained. I do not know how much I should go into general considerations.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should be very much interested in having some light on the price index.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean a comparison with that of the United States?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If that is what the hon. member wishes to have, I shall try to get some information along the lines requested by him. However I do not know whether it will be possible to get anything definite. I should think the revaluation of the dollar would have some influence, although not a very great one. It would not begin to account for the difference between the price rise in the United States and that in Canada. I shall also look into the subsidies situation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And exports.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Well, I do not think my hon. friend's point about lumber is a good one, at all. I think he was making his case the

Emergency Powers
other way around; that is, he has established that the existence of controls keeps prices down.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I may be handing the government a compliment on that export matter. But surely the minister will agree that if lumber, which is taken only as an example, is being sold on the Canadian market at less than the cost of production, the government would have to allow the price to be increased in order to make ends meet in the industry, if it were not for the fact that in a sense the industry is bonused by high prices in the export market. I am suggesting that, in connection with the comparison of prices of commodities included in the Canadian cost of living index, there is some unfairness when a comparison is made with the United States index.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I cannot see that point. I do not know whether domestic prices are less than the cost of production or not. I do not agree that they are; I do not know.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will find out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know whether I can or not; I do not believe I can.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I could soon find out from the department.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Last night in the midst of some discussion, to part of which exception was taken by the Minister of Justice, questions were put by the hon. member for Vancouver South to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, which the minister said were perfectly proper questions. They had to do with Nos. 56 and 57 in this list of fifty-seven orders in council. The nature of the question was this: Why are they included in this measure?
Taking that as my starting point, from the point of view of relevancy and order, I should like to sajr a word concerning an order also included among the fifty-seven which, in my submission, clears ought also to be the subject of a separate bill, and particularly in view of certain observations made in the speech from the throne. I refer to the subject of old age pensions.
We have among the orders in council a number which deal with the subject of old age pensions, the gist of which is to permit the addition of some $5 a month by way of subsidy to the present statutory rate fixed by the Old Age Pensions Act. In the speech from the throne, to be found on page 3 of Hansard there appears this sentence:
Amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act will be introduced at the present session.
We have had it put quite clearly before the committee that some time at this session the government is to introduce a bill to amend the Old Age Pensions Act. Is there any reason therefore why this omnibus bill to be introduced should contain, presumably for a temporary period, the orders in council which relate to this very matter? It was indicated in earlier discussion in the house this session that the purpose of the amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act would be to increase the basic rate of the pensions above the present S20 monthly statutory rate plus the $5 provided for under the orders in council.
Would it not be sensible to drop these orders from among the group of fifty-seven in the omnibus bill and make them part and parcel of whatever bill the government may decide to introduce to amend the act itself? Why should we be taking two bites of the cherry? The effect of these orders has now been extended to May 15. We are no longer faced with the situation which the government might have stated earlier as a reason for continuing these measures. Certainly, with the extension of the effect of these orders to May 15 there is ample time for the government to bring in its bill to amend the act and increase the rates on a statutory basis, without asking the house to take time meanwhile to go over a number of these orders and to give them the effect of statutes for the meantime.
Surely the sensible and businesslike way to go about this is to say that in view of the extension of these orders to May 15 the government should bring in its measure to amend the act and increase the statutory rate. We heard) something this afternoon from the Prime Minister about duplicating debate. Is there any better way of duplicating debate than the procedure the government is following in this respect? We all must seek to approach this matter in the most orderly way, in a way that will save time and bring us most directly to the meat of the problem. I submit that the government will be making a contribution in that direction if they will bring in their bill to amend the Old Age Pensions Act and increase the statutory rate. In that way they will dispense with any necessity for including the orders in council relating to old age pensions in the omnibus bill. Surely that bill will be loaded down enough without including measures that are to be the subject of duplicating legislation at a later stage in the session. Not only are we going to duplicate discussion, but apparently we are going to duplicate the legislation itself.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman-
Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would ask for some comment on these remarks of mine. I was not making them just for the sake of talking; I made them in the hope that they would be a contribution toward an orderly approach to the problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not know of any reason why the old age pensions legislation should not be brought in at as early a day as possible. It was quite obvious at the beginning of February that we would not be able to have the old age pensions legislation put through by March 31 and we attempted to avoid any hiatus. There are many considerations which I cannot outline to the committee. We had to keep in mind our dealings with the provinces. We had to have a little time on that and we knew we could not get it through by March 31. It might be possible to do it before May 15, but I do not know.
The same considerations apply to other legislation, such as the labour relations legislation. We have to get out of that field just as soon as we reasonably can and we have to have legislation about that this session. The existing orders in council are included under this measure although we are going to bring in legislation later in the session. That may mean duplication because it means making arrangements with all the provinces and giving them a chance to pass legislation. We knew we could not make the transfer to the provinces before March 31, but we might be able to do so before May 15. I shall have to speak to the Minister of Labour about that.
I would point out that we cannot do everything between now and May 15. We have not done anything yet except to deal with emergency legislation and the speech from the throne. We have quite a large sessional programme to go on with and we want to get a lot of this legislation through. If we start giving priority to everything, we shall not be able to do that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister clear up one point? I take it that it is not the intention of the government to continue the orders in council in relation to old age pensions beyond the date when the amendments come into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In other words, the government is simply proposing to continue these four orders in council which relate to old age pensions until it gets the bill amending the act through the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes.

Mr, FLEMING: The bill to be introduced will cover all the matters that are within the scope of the orders in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister tell us what orders in council are to be replaced by statutes during the present session? In his preliminary statement he said that some of these fifty-seven orders in council were administrative, some were regulative, and some were legislative. It would be of considerable help if we knew which of the orders in council he considers to be legislative.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There are three classes of orders in council. There are the orders in council relating to old age pensions; there are the orders in council relating to labour relations, and there are the orders in council relating to veterans preference. Those three classes of orders in council are to be replaced by legislation this session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There are five orders under the heading. Civil Service Commission; nine under the Department of Labour, and four dealing with old age pensions under the Department of National Health and Welfare. What orders in council are to be replaced by statutes? Will all those that I have mentioned be replaced in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I am asking which ones are to be replaced by legislation later in the
session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is ambiguous. I have had some experience in having my language examined rather closely and I am going to be somewhat careful. What the hon. gentleman is asking is whether these are to be revoked when the legislation dealing with the subject matter is passed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That would meet it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I could go over them and mark them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I do not think there will be any difficulty about that. Of course, once we give an undertaking to revoke we have to revoke. Certainly it is clear in my mind

exactly what we are intending to do. The principle of what we are intending to do is to enact old age pensions legislation, in which event these four orders in council relating to old age pensions would be revoked. That is No. 1. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Cannot the hon. gentleman apply the principle himself instead of trying to pin me down here to numbers of orders in council. I am giving the principle of the thing, which is quite clear. Then, third, are the orders in council relating to P.C. 1003?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Be extra careful on that.

The provinces, we assume, will pass legislation covering part of this field. The part occupied by ourselves will be greatly contracted, and our legislation will cover that contracted field. Then those parts of the order in council which are replaced by our legislation and by provincial legislation will be revoked. That is the principle of what we are going to do, and I think that ought to be sufficient.

speechtext: No; we are entitled to have that information now. I submit that if the minister is not prepared to complete his statement today he should do so tomorrow and tell us which other orders in council are to be revoked because legislation is to be brought in replacing them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I thank you, Mr. Chairman. Some time ago I started to ask a question of the right hon. minister and it provoked so much discussion that I have not been able to complete it. The right hon. gentleman said that the financing of the war had been achieved roughly one-half by taxation and two-sixths-I said two-sixths by borrowing and one-sixth by inflation. The right hon. gentleman did not quite agree with my description of the method resorted to for the last one-sixth. It does not make much difference what we call it. It was a way of puffing ourselves up by resorting to the printing press or to borrowings from the banks. Since I embarked upon this inquiry earlier in the afternoon I have been fortunate enough to get a couple of documents which will possibly enable me-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wonder how the hon. member relates this financial aspect of our war effort to the resolution now before us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman, that you had the good fortune to be absent when I started on this question. I said that the resolution took it for granted that there existed a national emergency. I am not convinced that such is the case, and inasmuch as the existence of a national emergency is the basis of the resolution I was inquiring into
Emergency Powers

certain features of the emergency referred to by the right hon. gentleman in his address which I thought should be supplemented by some additional information in order that we might deal with the resolution, as they say in that part of the country from which I come, en pleine connaissance de cause, which means with a little more information than you have at the present time. What I wanted to say was that the right hon. gentleman in his budget of 1943 said:
The plain fact is that this year we have had to depend too much on bank borrowing.
Then in the annual report for the year 1945 to the Minister of Finance and statement of accounts by the governor of the Bank of Canada I find this statement:
The remaining one-sixth-
That was the one-sixth of the cost of the war which had not been paid for out of taxation or borrowing. It was accounted for in this way:
The remaining one-sixth of the government's total requirements has been financed to a considerable extent by the chartered banks, which has involved a substantial increase in their holdings of government securities, and consequently in the volume of savings and demand deposits of the public with the banks.
This increase in deposit liabilities has in turn given rise to a need on the part of the chartered banks for larger cash reserves. The policy of the Bank of Canada-implemented through its purchase of government securities in the market-has been to keep pace with these necessities, without trying to bring about expansion of credit for purposes unrelated to war needs.
To a neophyte like myself that means a type of inflation. The question I wish to ask the minister-and1 upon the answer I think I can base the remainder of my argument-is, has not that device, whether it be called inflation or whether it be called by a more euphonious name, resulted in a reduction in the purchasing power value of the Canadian dollar?

speechtext: Does the minister not understand it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The answer to that question is not perfectly obvious, but my opinion is that the large increase in bank deposits during the war had an influence of driving the price level up; that what might be called inflation of credit and currency-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is that different, from currency circulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am talking about volume now; the volume of currency and credit in this country increased, and what might be called inflation of the volume of currency and credit in the country. My opinion is that that affected the inflation of prices; it caused some inflation of prices, but the two are different because perhaps one would not necessarily follow the other.
The reason I do not want to say "yes" to the question, did we resort to inflation as a device for financing the war is that it might be seriously misunderstood, it is so ambiguous. One hears about countries which pursue a policy of price inflation or might pursue a policy of encouraging price inflation so that their tax receipts will be much greater, so that they will get more money in that way, which might be a device of financing by inflation. I do not want to say "yes" to that at all.
